*Purpose*: We've been learning how to quantify uncertainty in estimates through the exercises; now its time to put those skills to use studying real data. In this challenge we'll use concepts like confidence intervals to help us make sense of census data.

*Reading*: - [Using ACS Estimates and Margin of Error](https://www.census.gov/data/academy/webinars/2020/calculating-margins-of-error-acs.html) (Optional, see the PDF on the page) - [Patterns and Causes of Uncertainty in the American Community Survey](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0143622813002518?casa_token=VddzQ1-spHMAAAAA:FTq92LXgiPVloJUVjnHs8Ma1HwvPigisAYtzfqaGbbRRwoknNq56Y2IzszmGgIGH4JAPzQN0) (Optional, particularly the *Uncertainty in surveys* section under the Introduction.)

```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)

#the probability that the confidence interval contains the value: it's either 0 or 1 because the value is either in the interval or not. 99% confidence is not necessarily a 99% probability that something will happen
#5 samples, compute sample mean and sample sd repeatedly, form confidence interval, every interval either does or does not include true value we're interested in
#confidence refers to theoretical procedure of repeatign sampling many many times and how many times are we going to include the true value 
#wider or narrower confidence intervals are based on the sample drawn, varies from case to case
#randomization used to remove sampling bias
#confounding variables are also hopefully removed with randomization
#really hard to list all the things that are confounding so randomization hopefully takes care of that
#Experimental study extra randomization: randomized assignment --> randomly get split into treatment and control 
#Randomization when drawing a sample --> supports inference: allows us to make statements at a specific confidence level about the population
#Randomization assignment --> supports causality: RCT, finding out what causes what
#how to pick a sample size when we're looking for differences between groups 
#randomly selecting: are we guaraunteed to get an equal number of squares vs triangles --> no 
#how to choose how to gather data really informs what you can do 
#characterize difference between groups: oversample a particularl group --> stratiying the sample
#take some # indiv from triangle and # indiv from square and make their standard error's similar (ex: sigma_sqr/sample_sqr or sigma_tri/sample_tri)
#Making SE's roughly equal, allocating resources to the thing that is more variable to become mroe confident in that quantity --> "greater statistical power" to find differences if they exist
#Assuming that the two groups have the same variability if you're just going off the make the sample sizes equal, weak and fragile rule of thumb 
#how do you balance SE --> you don't know SD until you collect all your data --> infinite statistical regress 
#Go to existing literature, do we tend to see any differences in how variable a population is --> one twice as variable as another, looking for equality, all you need to know is how proportionally different they are, can control the SD more and then allows for the sqrt(sample size) to be more constrained
#Populations are frequently not actually normal 
#Median = Q50% sometimes, not standard greek variable
#CLT will break down quickly if moving to a different statistic
#Bootstrap will not break down --> helper function in c07
#Statistic: summary quantity summarizing a population --> mean, sd computed, have both a population version and a sample version
#Means of different groups: actually studying delta = mu_sqr - mu_tri
#Compute a CI on this delta quantity --> delta_hat = mu_sqrhat - mu_trihat
#Difference can be in the negatives or positive --> include 0 
#CI negative, delta < 0, squares less income than triangles
#"Epistemologically diffuse" what the heck does that even mean --> fancy way of saying bad 
#Confidence interval that includes 0 --> guarunatees that we don't have evidence to support a conclusion that one income of one group is more or less than the other --> might be incentivized for things to come out more one way than another (ex: new treatment vs standard of care)
#Significant difference: confidence interval does not include zero when we are considering two statistics of interests
#Sometimes prefer for things to come out similar --> ex: income, differences in income show differences between groups 
#Generally want CI's to be narrower --> ways to get them narrower?
#One thing has higher SD, put more observational units to stamp down the SE --> pooled standard deviation, scale sd by sample sizes chosen then do renormalization to "put them back together", put more observations into one group because indiv sample sizes are combining --> standardized difference: Cohen's d
#Multiple testing ?????
#two groups "strongly separated" relative to their SD's, how far apart their SD's are d = (mu_sqrhat - mu_trihat) / s, less overalp means huge difference, more overlap means larger difference, may need thousands of samples to get this difference
#Target power: probability that we would actually go out and find the difference in a population
#Significance value = alpha
#Need larger amounts of difference to make it statistically significant --> difference too small then just talk about what kind of conclusions your data can endorse
```

### **q1** Load the population data from c06; simply replace `filename_pop` below.

```{r q1-task}
## TODO: Give the filename for your copy of Table B01003
filename_pop <- "C:/Users/sjalinous/Data-Science-2026-/data-science-curriculum-build/challenges/ACSDT5Y2018.B01003_2026-10-15T105154/ACSDT5Y2018.B01003-Data.csv"

## NOTE: No need to edit
df_pop <-
  read_csv(
    filename_pop,
    skip = 1,
  ) %>% 
  rename(
    population_estimate = `Estimate!!Total`
  )

df_pop
```

You might wonder why the `Margin of Error` in the population estimates is listed as `*****`. From the [documentation (PDF link)](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=&cad=rja&uact=8&ved=2ahUKEwj81Omy16TrAhXsguAKHTzKDQEQFjABegQIBxAB&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww2.census.gov%2Fprograms-surveys%2Facs%2Ftech_docs%2Faccuracy%2FMultiyearACSAccuracyofData2018.pdf%3F&usg=AOvVaw2TOrVuBDlkDI2gde6ugce_) for the ACS:

> If the margin of error is displayed as ‘\*\*\*\*\*’ (five asterisks), the estimate has been controlled to be equal to a fixed value and so it has no sampling error. A standard error of zero should be used for these controlled estimates when completing calculations, such as those in the following section.

This means that for cases listed as `*****` the US Census Bureau recommends treating the margin of error (and thus standard error) as zero.

- `Filter > Geography > County > All counties in United States`
- Look for `Median Income in the Past 12 Months` (Table S1903)
- Download the 2018 5-year ACS estimates; save to your `data` folder and add the filename below.


```{r q2-tests}
assertthat::assert_that(
```

This dataset is in desperate need of some *tidying*. To simplify the task, we'll start by considering the `\\d-person families` columns first.

### **q3** Tidy the `df_income` dataset by completing the code below. Pivot and rename the columns to arrive at the column names `id, geographic_area_name, category, income_estimate, income_moe`.

*Hint*: You can do this in a single pivot using the `".value"` argument and a `names_pattern` using capture groups `"()"`. Remember that you can use an OR operator `|` in a regex to allow for multiple possibilities in a capture group, for example `"(Estimate|Margin of Error)"`.

```{r q3-task}
df_q3 <-
  df_income %>%
  select(
    Geography,
    contains("Geographic"),
    # This will select only the numeric d-person family columns;
    # it will ignore the annotation columns
    contains("median") & matches("\\d-person families") & !contains("Annotation of")
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(contains("median"), as.numeric)) %>%
## TODO: Pivot the data, rename the columns
  pivot_longer(
    names_to = c(".value","category"),
    names_pattern = "(Estimate|Margin of Error).*(\\d-person families)",
    cols = -c("Geography", "Geographic Area Name")
  ) %>%
  rename(
    "geographic_area_name" = "Geographic Area Name",
    "income_estimate" = "Estimate",
    "income_moe" = "Margin of Error"
    )
df_q3
```

Use the following tests to check your work:

```{r q3-tests}
## NOTE: No need to edit
assertthat::assert_that(setequal(
  names(df_q3),
  c("Geography", "geographic_area_name", "category", "income_estimate", "income_moe")
))

assertthat::assert_that(
  df_q3 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_moe)
  == 6663
)

print("Nice!")
```

The data gives finite values for the Margin of Error, which is closely related to the Standard Error. The Census Bureau documentation gives the following relationship between Margin of Error and Standard Error:

$$\text{MOE} = 1.645 \times \text{SE}.$$

### **q4** Convert the margin of error to standard error. Additionally, compute a 99% confidence interval on income, and normalize the standard error to `income_CV = income_SE / income_estimate`. Provide these columns with the names `income_SE, income_lo, income_hi, income_CV`.

```{r q4-task}

df_q4 <-
  df_q3 %>%
  mutate(
    income_SE = income_moe / 1.645,
    income_CV = income_SE / income_estimate,
    income_lo = income_estimate - 2.576*income_SE,
    income_hi = income_estimate + 2.576*income_SE
  )
df_q4
# lo_q1 <- mean(z_q1) - qnorm( 1 - (1 - 0.99) / 2 ) * sd(z_q1) / sqrt(100)
# hi_q1 <- mean(z_q1) + qnorm( 1 - (1 - 0.99) / 2 ) * sd(z_q1) / sqrt(100)
```

Use the following tests to check your work:

```{r q4-tests}
## NOTE: No need to edit
assertthat::assert_that(setequal(
  names(df_q4),
  c("Geography", "geographic_area_name", "category", "income_estimate", "income_moe",
    "income_SE", "income_lo", "income_hi", "income_CV")
))

assertthat::assert_that(
  abs(
    df_q4 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_SE) - 4050.456
  ) / 4050.456 < 1e-3
)

assertthat::assert_that(
  abs(
    df_q4 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_lo) - 54513.72
  ) / 54513.72 < 1e-3
)

assertthat::assert_that(
  abs(
    df_q4 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_hi) - 75380.28
  ) / 75380.28 < 1e-3
)

assertthat::assert_that(
  abs(
    df_q4 %>%
    filter(Geography == "0500000US01001", category == "2-person families") %>%
    pull(income_CV) - 0.06236556
  ) / 0.06236556 < 1e-3
)

print("Nice!")
```

# Analysis

<!-- ----------------------------------------------------------------------- -->

We now have both estimates and confidence intervals for `\\d-person families`. Now we can compare cases with quantified uncertainties: Let's practice!

### **q6** Study the following graph, making sure to note what you can *and can't* conclude based on the estimates and confidence intervals. Document your observations below and answer the questions.

```{r q6-task}
## NOTE: No need to edit; run and inspect
wid <- 0.5

df_data %>%
  filter(str_detect(geographic_area_name, "Massachusetts")) %>%
  mutate(
    county = str_remove(geographic_area_name, " County,.*$"),
    county = fct_reorder(county, income_estimate)
  ) %>%

  ggplot(aes(county, income_estimate, color = category)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = income_lo, ymax = income_hi),
    position = position_dodge(width = wid)
  ) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = wid)) +

  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    x = "County",
    y = "Median Household Income"
  )
```

**Observations**:

- Document your observations here.
  - The confidence intervals for the 2-person families are consistently very small.
  - Nantucket has an insane confidence intervals for the 5-person families. This may be due to the small population due to Nantucket being an island.
  - Dukes has a similar issue with the confidence intervals as Nantucket, but it is a bit less pronounced and it's once again probably caused by a small island population.
  - The larger the families, the larger the confidence intervals tend to be.
  - Shockingly, the households with less people tend to have less median income.
- Can you confidently distinguish between household incomes in Suffolk county? Why or why not?
  - No because their confidence intervals are all over each other so they could all be somewhere else and are too overlapping to be distinct.
- Which counties have the widest confidence intervals?
  - Nantucket, Dukes, Hampshire

In the next task you'll investigate the relationship between population and uncertainty.

### **q7** Plot the standard error against population for all counties. Create a visual that effectively highlights the trends in the data. Answer the questions under *observations* below.

*Hint*: Remember that standard error is a function of *both* variability (e.g. variance) and sample size.

```{r q7-task}
df_data %>%
  ggplot(
    aes(population_estimate, income_SE)
  ) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10()
```

**Observations**:

- What *overall* trend do you see between `SE` and population? Why might this trend exist?
  - As population increases, standard error becomes more precise. This trend might exist because the closer you get to portraying the full population in your data, the less error you tend to have.
- What does this *overall* trend tell you about the relative ease of studying small vs large counties?
  - It is relatively easier to study larger counties because there are more samples available to you, whereas smaller counties it is harder to get the same number of samples to be as precise.

**Observations**:

- Norfolk county has the highest income estimate, but by very little when compared to Middlesex county. They are pretty similar. Worcester, on the other hand, has a lower income estimate overall. I grew up in Middlesex county and then we moved to Worcester county after I finished high school because it is cheaper, which is corroborated by this graph. It also makes sense that Norfolk and Middlesex are virtually the same, because I forgot Needham was even in Norfolk county and thought it was in Middlesex county because they're so similar. But I would never thing Worcester county is the same because there is a distinct difference in that county compared to the other two.
- One other curious thing is that in Middlesex and Worcester county, 4-person families have the largest income, which is surprising because you'd think that income would go up with more people in the family.
